questions.q: Why does `WHERE SUM(invoice_amount) > 50000` fail in Oracle SQL?
options: SUM cannot be used anywhere in a query
50000 is not a valid number for comparison
WHERE is evaluated before grouping/aggregation happens, so there is no aggregated value yet for it to filter on
WHERE can only be used with text columns
questions.explain: WHERE filters individual rows before GROUP BY aggregates them, so it cannot reference an aggregate result like SUM(invoice_amount).

questions.q: What is HAVING specifically designed to do?
options: Filter groups after aggregation, based on the aggregate value
Filter individual rows before grouping
Sort the final result set
Join two tables together
questions.explain: HAVING runs after GROUP BY has produced its one-row-per-group result, allowing filters on aggregate values like SUM or COUNT.

questions.q: What is Oracle's logical clause evaluation order for a query with FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING and ORDER BY?
options: ORDER BY, HAVING, GROUP BY, WHERE, FROM
WHERE, FROM, HAVING, GROUP BY, ORDER BY
GROUP BY, FROM, WHERE, ORDER BY, HAVING
FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, ORDER BY
questions.explain: Regardless of typed order, Oracle evaluates FROM, then WHERE, then GROUP BY, then HAVING, then ORDER BY.

questions.q: In `... WHERE payment_status_flag <> 'Y' GROUP BY vendor_id HAVING COUNT(*) >= 3;`, what does WHERE do versus HAVING?
options: WHERE and HAVING do the exact same thing in this query
WHERE picks which rows count as not-fully-paid; HAVING keeps only suppliers with 3 or more such rows
HAVING filters rows before grouping; WHERE filters the aggregate
WHERE is ignored once HAVING is present
questions.explain: WHERE filters at the row level (which invoices count), while HAVING filters at the group level (which suppliers have enough qualifying rows).

questions.q: Why is it generally more efficient to filter rows with WHERE rather than relying only on HAVING when possible?
options: HAVING is not valid Oracle syntax
WHERE and HAVING always produce different, unrelated results
WHERE narrows down rows before grouping happens, so fewer rows need to be grouped and aggregated at all
There is no efficiency difference between the two
questions.explain: Filtering with WHERE reduces the row set before the (often more expensive) grouping and aggregation work happens.
